How to Raise for an Emerging Tech Company: The Complete Guide

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 14-minute read · Strategy

Raising for an emerging tech company in 2026 means raising in a market with record totals and narrow access. US venture deal value reached $515.8 billion through September, but rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of first-half dollars, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion year on year. The companies that raise normal-sized rounds do four things: they raise against evidence, not narrative; they run the round like a sales process; they read pass reasons when it stalls; and they adjust for what their category changes, whether that is inference cost, a licence, a long sales cycle or a platform-dependent audience.

This guide is operating and commercial guidance, not investment, legal or regulatory advice. lowob advises on narrative and readiness; it doesn't arrange, value or negotiate rounds, act as a placement agent or take a percentage of anything raised.

The market in late 2026: record totals, narrow access

Start with the numbers, because they explain why most of the advice in this guide is about proof.

The Q3 2026 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor recorded $515.8 billion of US venture deal value through September, about 44% above the full-year record set in 2021. AI companies took 82.7% of it. Globally, Crunchbase counted a record $510 billion in the first half, of which OpenAI and Anthropic together took $217 billion, or 43%. Foley & Lardner's summary of Crunchbase's third-quarter data shows $159 billion invested in the quarter, with roughly a third going to 27 companies that raised rounds of $1 billion or more.

Underneath the totals, access is narrow. PitchBook's second-quarter report found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the US in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024. Carta, which sees rounds raised by companies on its platform, recorded seed capital falling from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and Series B capital falling from $13.5 billion to $10.4 billion.

The supply of funds is concentrating too. Through September, funds of $500 million or more took 78.1% of US venture fundraising while making up 6.0% of funds closed, and only 81 first-time funds closed, on pace for a decade low. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that emerging managers who raised in 2021 or 2022 had likely used most of their dry powder.

Not every signal is negative. PitchBook expects a record number of US first financings in 2026. Carta's down-round rate fell to 11.4% in the first quarter, the lowest in nearly four years. Hardware capital on Carta's platform rose from $8.6 billion to $14.3 billion year on year. Capital is available. It is going to companies that have already removed some risk.

What each stage is buying

Every round buys a specific proof. Knowing which one your round is buying sets the evidence, the investor list and the size.

StageMedian post-money on Carta, Q1 2026What the round is buyingEvidence investors weight most
Pre-seedNot reported in the Q1 reportA founder and a sharp problemFounder-market fit, 5 to 10 named people who would use it
Seed$21.6 millionProof that someone uses itDesign partners with usage, early retention, a few paying users
Series A$63 millionProof that it repeatsRepeatable acquisition, recurring revenue, a channel that scales
Series B$177 millionProof that it scales efficientlyRetention, margin and payback at a larger base

Two facts follow from Carta's data. First, the price roughly triples between seed and Series A, so a Series A investor is paying for proof that seed-stage evidence repeated. Second, Carta's median gap is two years from seed to Series A and 2.1 years from Series A to Series B. A round has to fund the company until the next proof exists, plus the time to raise again.

Valuations are also splitting by category. PitchBook data reported in August 2026 shows AI companies posting a median valuation step-up of 2.2x in 2026 against 1.6x for non-AI companies, and companies that last raised in 2021 trading at a median 59.1% discount on secondary markets. A company still carrying a 2021 price is raising against that price as well as against its evidence.

Evidence before narrative

Raise against evidence, not narrative is the core argument of this guide. Investors price risk. Narrative asks them to imagine the risk away; evidence removes some of it. Even a small amount of real evidence changes which investors take the call, how fast they move and what they ask for.

Evidence is what a non-founder has done with the product. Keep it in one dated evidence log with five lines: usage, quotes, commitments, community work done by people you did not pay, and losses with reasons. The log is the source for the deck, the data room and customer case studies. Because the median gap to the next round is two years, write each entry so that someone who was not there can understand it.

Three kinds of activity look like evidence and are not:

  • Paid-for activity. Points programmes, airdrops and incentive campaigns produce numbers that look like adoption until the incentive stops.
  • Demos. A demo proves a model can do something once. Investors want to see a customer let it do the job every day.
  • Free usage. Free-tier activity is acquisition cost, not demand.

Put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3, before the market slide, and let the market slide answer the question it raises: how many more buyers look like this one? DocSend's pitch deck index recorded investors spending an average of about two and a half minutes per deck in 2023 and 2024. Evidence that sits on slide 11 may not be read.

When there is no evidence yet, the honest move is to raise less, from investors who back founders at the idea stage, or to spend four to six weeks getting first evidence. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

Capital is available in 2026. It is going to companies that have already removed some risk.

Running the round like a sales process

Run the round like a sales process treats investors as accounts. The steps are the ones a good sales team follows.

  1. Build a fit-first list. A fund fits if it has invested at your stage and in your category in the last 12 months, and has room in its current fund. Aim for 40 to 60 named funds with a written reason for each, in two tiers. Check the year each fund closed: a fund raised in 2021 may be reserving what it has left for its existing portfolio.
  2. Research the partner, not the firm. Find the person who invests in your area and name one specific reason you are relevant to them.
  3. Get in warm. The best route is a founder in their portfolio who knows your product. Send the introducer a forwardable three-line email: who you are, what you've proven, why this investor.
  4. Compress the window. Run first meetings within two to three weeks. Overlapping interest creates urgency; a raise that drips out over four months signals that nobody wants it.
  5. Track a pipeline. Researched, intro requested, first meeting, deep dive, term sheet, passed. Log every pass reason in the investor's words.
  6. Have the data room ready before meeting one. Deck, one-page memo, model, cap table and token allocation, evidence log, audits or security reviews, and two or three reference customers.

Separate investor types before writing a word. Crypto-native funds, generalists with a crypto practice and ecosystem funds want different stories, and ecosystem money often wants deployment on its chain. AI infrastructure funds and AI application funds price on different logic. Tier 1 funds come second, after a week of practice in Tier 2 meetings.

When the round stalls

The round has stalled sets out the diagnosis. A stalled round is a process fault or an evidence gap, and the pass reasons tell you which. The five usual faults are: pass reasons never logged, a window that dripped, Tier 1 pitched first, diligence that waited on the founder, and a real evidence gap.

Read every pass in the investor's own words and count the matches. If three match, that is the gap: fix it in weeks and relaunch, or pause the round, tell the live funds why and name a return date. If nothing repeats, the fault is process: put every live conversation in a two-week window, tell each fund the date, finish the data room and answer every homework request within 48 hours.

Two moves rarely help. Widening the list to hundreds of names produces more passes, not more offers. Cutting the price does not supply missing evidence, and with down rounds at 11.4% of rounds on Carta in the first quarter, a cut is now the exception and reads as distress. The exception to the exception is a company still priced at a 2021 valuation, where the pass reasons usually name the price.

AI companies: priced like software, plus two costs

Raising for an AI company starts from a split. Model companies are priced on capability, compute and research talent. Application companies are priced like software companies, on retention, margin, distribution and replaceability, with two extra costs: inference, which hits gross margin, and platform risk, because the provider can ship your feature.

The label no longer differentiates. Carta found 60.7% of capital raised on its platform in the first quarter of 2026 went to AI companies, and 83% of SaaS capital went to those building with AI. Investors ask five questions early: gross margin after inference, what happens when the provider ships your feature, switching cost between models, data rights in customer contracts, and how much usage is paid.

Switching has become a live question. Menlo Ventures' November 2026 enterprise survey, which is investor research, found Anthropic's share of enterprise API spend rose from 40% to 55% in a year while Google's fell from 21% to 9%. A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could. Lead with the customer and the workflow; the model and eval results go in the appendix. Credits are a cost reduction with an expiry date, never revenue.

Regulated categories: trust and durability

Raising in a regulated category argues that fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Four things change the raise.

The licence is an asset. A granted licence shows a regulator said yes and sets the time a competitor needs to catch up. Davis Wright Tremaine's August 2026 review traced one de novo US national bank from application in December 2025 to conditional OCC approval in May 2026, and recorded conditional OCC approvals for fintechs including Mercury and Upstart and final approval for Circle's national trust bank in July 2026. In the UK, the FCA reported that new firm and payment services authorisations both missed their service targets in April to June 2026. Show the path with dates, budget and a named owner.

The unit is the funded account. Build acquisition cost, revenue and payback per funded account, and state the sign-up to funded ratio.

Compliance and losses get their own model lines, with trends and the control changes that moved them.

The partner bank question gets one slide. After the 2024 bankruptcy of Synapse, the FDIC proposed recordkeeping and reconciliation rules for fintech custodial accounts, and banks already apply the 2023 interagency third-party risk guidance to their fintech partners. Investors will ask who the partner is, what they control, what is concentrated, who holds the ledger and what the exit plan is.

For crypto companies the regulatory path is still moving. PitchBook's second-quarter report noted the US CLARITY Act had cleared the Senate Banking Committee but still lacked a floor vote, and the OCC granted conditional national trust charters to several digital asset firms in December 2025. Treat any charter or registration the business depends on the same way: dated, budgeted and owned.

Long cycles: milestones, not time

Raising for long cycles covers robotics, compute, energy and other companies whose pilots take a year and procurement another. The round is sized to the next milestone that makes the company worth more, and each round retires one named risk: technical de-risking in a real deployment, a paying pilot, or regulatory clearance.

The capital stack is layered, and each layer carries a different risk. Non-dilutive money funds what investors will not yet, but it is slow: US SBIR and STTR authority lapsed for six months before reauthorisation to 2031 on 13 April 2026, according to the Congressional Research Service. Project finance funds proven units only. Mayer Brown's guide to the US Office of Energy Dominance Financing notes a preferred technology readiness level of 8 and that research, pilot and demonstration projects will be denied. Runway must cover the full sales cycle plus about six months to raise again.

Revenue models for long cycles is the companion piece. Choose the model by who carries the capital and the service tail; measure gross margin per unit including service from the first deployment; price pilots as projects with a conversion price; write production contracts with terms a lender can read. Report converted pilots and contracted annual value, never letters of intent.

Media: repeat revenue, not reach

What investors fund in media now applies the evidence argument to audiences. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% in a year. Its Digital News Report 2026 found about 17% of people across 20 countries pay for online news. Investors fund owned audiences that pay, proprietary data, licensing with signed terms, events with margins and software on the audience, and they read renewal before growth.

Fundraising is one part of one system

The Raise, Rally, Revenue series puts fundraising at steps three and four of a ten-step order: name the buyer, write one truth, collect evidence, raise against it, give the community a job, recruit the first hundred, make first customers design partners, distribute, measure, hand over. Most fundraising problems are problems earlier in that order. A round that stalls on "want to see traction" is a design partner problem. A deck that lands with investors but not customers is a product truth problem.

The order matters more than any tactic. Every failure in the series came from doing a right thing at the wrong time.

lowob takeaways

  • Read the market as concentrated, not closed. Capital goes to companies that have already removed some risk.
  • Know what your round is buying. Each stage buys a different proof, and the next round is about two years away.
  • Raise against evidence. Keep a dated log, strip out paid-for activity and put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3.
  • Run a pipeline, not a drip. Fit-first list, warm routes, a two-to-three-week window and every pass logged.
  • Adjust for the category, keep the process. Inference, licences, long cycles and audiences change the proof, not the method.
Gateway card

Before you send the first investor email

  • A dated evidence log, with paid-for activity separated from organic activity
  • The proof this round buys, and the milestone the next round needs, written down
  • 40 to 60 named funds with recent deals at your stage and capital in the current fund
  • A forwardable three-line introduction email
  • First meetings planned inside a two-to-three-week window
  • A pipeline tracker with a column for pass reasons in the investor's words
  • A complete data room, including the category-specific shelf: inference margins, licences and partner agreements, or deployment data

Next move

Write one sentence that names the proof your next round is buying, then list the three strongest entries in your evidence log that support it. If you cannot fill the list, spend the next four to six weeks on evidence before you contact an investor.
